name: ZAP MCP add-on
description: ZAP add-ons repo; the MCP Integration add-on lets AI assistants drive ZAP spider/active scans
scored_configuration: MCP Integration add-on 0.4.0 with the listener enabled by the operator and otherwise default options (security key required, HTTPS only, history recording off).
headline: The server is off until enabled and, once on, requires a random key over HTTPS, but it then exposes ZAP's full capability to any key holder: unrestricted active scans and spidering of any URL, report writes to any path, and unredacted target traffic. It gives the host no risk annotations, previews or limits to gate on, and it returns target-controlled content with no provenance. Treat it as a localhost-only tool for a trusted client that must be approved at the host.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: The add-on holds no downstream credentials of its own; every tool runs with the full authority of the ZAP process that hosts it. Callers are authenticated with one randomly generated 32-character key compared in constant time and the listener is HTTPS-only by default, but there is no per-tool, per-user or read/write separation: whoever has the key can start scans, change contexts, write report files and read all recorded traffic. The key check can be switched off by an options change or by an empty key in the config job, and the server itself is off until the operator enables it.
criteria.notes: No token passthrough: the key is checked locally and is not forwarded; the importer sends a user-supplied key to the MCP server under test, which is an operator-driven job rather than a model-reachable tool.

S.finding: Authority is a single static shared key over ambient ZAP authority; no scoped roles, read-only credential, or per-tool narrowing.
S.gap: No role or per-capability scoping (read tools and write tools share one credential).

C.finding: Every JSON-RPC call (tools, resources, prompts) passes the same single authentication check in the HTTP handler before dispatch.
C.gap: Only authentication, not authorization: no per-tool or per-principal policy is evaluated, and the key is not tied to a requesting principal.

D.finding: Default posture is reasonable: server disabled, key required, random key generated on first load, HTTPS-only, bound to ZAP default address (inferred loopback).
D.gap: Widening is an operator config change without warning (options panel or an empty key in the config job turns the key requirement off).

B.finding: A compromised or leaked key gives full control of one system (ZAP): scans, scope changes, report file writes and read access to recorded traffic; independent layers are the opt-in server, HTTPS-only and localhost bind (the bind address lives in another add-on and was not verified).
B.gap: Full ZAP control is reachable with one key; no read-only mode or per-capability credential narrows it.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: The server gives the host no risk signalling to build an approval gate on. Tool listings carry only a name, description and input schema, with no read-only or destructive hints, and there is no dry-run, preview or server-side read-only mode. Read, start and stop operations are at least split into separate, clearly named tools, but a host cannot tell that zap_generate_report writes an arbitrary file or that zap_start_active_scan attacks a live target without reading descriptions.
criteria.notes: Tool-server anchors used: the host owns the gate. C2-POWERBYPASS not applied separately because the server has no gate to bypass and the cap would not bind (total is below 0.30).

S.finding: Tool listing exposes only name, description and inputSchema; no risk annotations of any kind.
S.gap: No accurate readOnlyHint/destructiveHint on any tool (L2 needs them on every tool).

evidence.note: no annotation fields anywhere in main sources

C.finding: No tool carries any signal the host could gate on; mutating tools (active scan, report write, context replace) are indistinguishable by protocol from read tools.
C.gap: Every mutating tool would need a flag or annotation for the host to gate on.

D.finding: No server-enforced confirmation or approval mode exists, on or off; approval is entirely the host's job.
D.gap: No server-side confirmation step or read-only mode that a host must complete.

evidence.note: no approval, confirmation or dry-run handling in main sources

B.gap: No dry-run or preview for destructive or outward-facing operations and no rate limits on them.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Argument handling is mostly presence checks and syntax parsing. Scan targets are only parsed as URIs; there is no host allowlist, scope check or internal-address blocking, and the report tool takes any file path. The one tool with real validation is the history reader, which allowlists field names, parses integers and windows large bodies. All 17 tools, including write and active-scan tools, are always registered with no way to enable only a read-only subset.

S.finding: Validation is syntactic: required-argument checks and URI parsing; only get_history uses an allowlist and bounds; targets, regexes, policy and report path are unconstrained.
S.gap: No allowlist or containment on target hosts or report path; no internal-address blocking.

C.finding: Only the history tool validates against an allowlist; others check presence and URI syntax only; tool schemas type every property as string or string array.
C.gap: Most tools do not apply real validation; no shared validation layer.

D.finding: All 17 tools including write, report and active-scan tools are registered unconditionally; there is no option to disable individual tools or select a read-only group.
D.gap: No read-only default tool set or per-tool enablement switch.

evidence.note: no per-tool enablement setting in McpParam or elsewhere

B.finding: Tools are fixed-function (scan, spider, report, history read) but their destinations are unbounded: any URL can be scanned or spidered and any path written.
B.gap: No target scope limits, quantity limits or path containment; destinations unbounded.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: No model-reachable path in this add-on interprets text as code: there is no shell, process spawn, script engine, dynamic class loading or eval in the main sources, and the tools only build fixed automation jobs (spider, AJAX spider, active scan) and call the report generator. The shipped extender-script templates are run only if the operator enables them in ZAP's scripting add-on. The scanner itself sends test requests to targets, which is outbound traffic scored under tool scoping and untrusted input, not local code execution.
criteria.notes: Absence by design, not a control. Regex arguments are compiled as patterns and passed to ZAP contexts, not evaluated as code.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: The server returns content that originates from scanned targets, including HTTP bodies and headers from history and alert evidence, as plain text or JSON with no provenance or untrusted marker, and offers no read-only or no-egress mode. A hijacked model reading that content can start spiders or active scans against any URL, which is both an outbound channel and an irreversible action on third parties, and can write report files, all without any server-side approval. The tool descriptions themselves are static and contain no directives.

cap.reason: B is L0: leaked traffic data and irreversible scans or file writes are reachable with no server-side human step.

S.finding: Outputs are plain text or JSON with no source or untrusted flag; get_history and resources do separate fields but nothing marks body content as target-controlled.
S.gap: No provenance or untrusted flag on returned content, and no mode that drops a Rule-of-Two leg.

evidence.note: no untrusted-content marking in main sources

C.finding: No untrusted source is distinguished: history bodies, alert evidence and site-tree data from targets enter the model context with the same standing as status output.
C.gap: Sources such as history bodies, alert evidence and sites data would need provenance handling.

D.finding: No mitigating mode exists to be on or off by default.
D.gap: No default control; nothing to be on by default.

evidence.note: no restrictive modes in main sources

B.finding: If a hijack succeeds, target-controlled text can steer unattended scans or spidering of arbitrary URLs (a data-carrying egress channel plus actions that cannot be undone on third-party systems) and report file writes, with nothing server-side requiring a human.
B.gap: No egress or state-change restriction after untrusted content has been read; destinations unrestricted.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: The add-on does not load instruction files or project config from the working directory, but state the model can change persists inside the ZAP session: zap_create_context and the scan tools create contexts that define scan scope, and an existing context with the same name is deleted and replaced without any check, including contexts the operator set up. Nothing validates or gates these writes and nothing logs them. Persisted contexts affect later scans started by any client.
criteria.notes: Configuration (key, port, enable flag) is changeable only through ZAP options or the automation config job, not through an MCP tool.

S.finding: Context writes by tools are neither validated nor gated, and an existing context of the same name is deleted first; no provenance or approval.
S.gap: Writes are not gated or validated and carry no provenance; replacing an operator context is silent.

C.finding: One persistent surface (session contexts) with no control; no instruction-file or repo-config auto-loading was found.
C.gap: The context store is uncontrolled; protections would need to cover every write path (create_context and scan tools).

evidence.note: no auto-loaded instruction files or env files

D.finding: Contexts are one global namespace in the ZAP session shared by all MCP clients and the operator; any client can overwrite any context by name.
D.gap: No per-client namespace; model can overwrite operator-created contexts.

B.finding: A replaced or widened context persists in the session and changes the scope of every later scan, which can be triggered by any client without a gate.
B.gap: Persisted context changes are not reviewed or reversible by the server.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: The add-on does not launch or download any third-party code: it starts no MCP server subprocesses, fetches no remote tools or models, and installs no packages. The importer only connects to an MCP server the operator names, as a test target. The tool registry is public, so other ZAP add-ons or operator-enabled extender scripts in the same process can register tools with full ZAP authority, which is ZAP's own extension model and is not verified or gated by this add-on.
criteria.notes: Absence by design. Residual: McpToolRegistry.registerTool is public and unauthenticated for in-process callers, so any other loaded ZAP add-on or enabled script can add tools; not scored as a control.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: The security key is stored in ZAP's configuration as plaintext and shown and copyable in the options panel; there is no masking or redaction anywhere. Request and response payloads are logged only at debug level, and request recording into ZAP history is off by default. Tool and resource results return target traffic unredacted, including headers that may hold session tokens or credentials of the tested application. No telemetry beyond local counters was found.
criteria.notes: C8-MODELSECRETS not applied: the server's own key is never sent to the model; target traffic is returned only on request. Not examined: how ZAP core stores config.xml permissions.

S.finding: Key generated with SecureRandom but kept as a plain config string; no masking, redaction or secret scanning in any path.
S.gap: No secret manager, encryption at rest or redaction before model-bound output.

evidence.note: no redaction helpers in main sources

C.finding: No path is protected: debug logs record request and response bodies unredacted, and history tools return headers and bodies as-is; the key is not logged only because the logging statements do not print headers.
C.gap: No log, model-bound or error path has redaction.

D.finding: Debug-level payload logging and history recording are off by default and no telemetry exists; redaction does not exist so cannot be left on.
D.gap: Redaction is absent rather than always on; stored data is not minimised.

B.finding: The key is long-lived, rotatable by the operator, and grants full control of ZAP; target secrets in history reach the model only when a tool or resource asks for them.
B.gap: Key is long-lived and full-scope rather than scoped and short-lived.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Tool calls are not recorded by default beyond debug-level log lines and per-tool success and failure counters that carry no arguments or caller. An optional setting records each MCP HTTP exchange, including rejected requests, into ZAP history with full request and response, which would give a structured record of calls, but it is off by default, has no actor or approver attribution, does not cover the event-stream GET path, and is best-effort. The model has no tool to delete history, but the record lives in the same ZAP session it can read.
criteria.notes: Counters via Stats.incCounter are aggregate and carry no arguments.

cap.reason: The only structured record of tool calls (history recording) is opt-in.

S.finding: When enabled, every POST exchange is stored in ZAP history with its full JSON-RPC request, response and timestamp.
S.gap: No actor attribution, approver or correlation IDs, and no tamper-evident or exported storage.

C.finding: The handler records successful and rejected requests (auth, HTTPS, method, empty body) but the GET event-stream path returns without recording.
C.gap: Not every path is recorded, and there are no approval or config-change records.

D.finding: Recording is off by default; default observability is debug-level logging and counters only.
D.gap: Recording would need to be on by default.

B.finding: History insertion is best-effort and does not gate execution; the call has already run when it is recorded.
B.gap: Records are not durable per action and high-risk actions do not wait for the record.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: The server enforces few bounds on its own work. The history tool defaults to a 4000-character body window but the caller can raise it, scans have no server-side time, concurrency or count limits, and resources are returned in full. Scan start waits at most 10 seconds for an ID, which bounds waiting rather than work. Stop tools exist for spider, AJAX spider and active scan and cancel the running job, which is the main damage-limiting control.
criteria.notes: Request-body size limits in the shared network add-on were not examined.

S.finding: Limits are mostly optional or caller-adjustable: max_body_chars has a default but can be raised; the 10-second wait does not bound the scan itself.
S.gap: No server-enforced ceilings on scan duration, concurrency or output size.

evidence.note: no rate or concurrency limiters

C.finding: Only a couple of tools have any bound; started scans, spiders and resource reads run without server caps.
C.gap: Scans and background plans are not counted against any budget.

D.finding: The one default (4000 body characters) can be raised by the caller; no other defaults exist.
D.gap: Defaults the caller cannot raise and sensible scan ceilings.

B.finding: There is no ceiling on how many scans can be started or how long they run; stopping a scan cancels the job but only on an explicit call, and stopping the server was not shown to cancel running plans.
B.gap: No tight time or count ceilings; no automatic stop.

fixes.summary: Add readOnlyHint/destructiveHint annotations to every tool so hosts can gate scans, context replacement and report writes.
Restrict scan targets to operator-configured scope or contexts and contain report paths to a configured directory.
Record every tool call (arguments, result, caller) by default outside the model's reach.
Return target-derived content with provenance and an untrusted flag, and offer a read-only mode.
Add server-side caps on concurrent scans and scan duration that callers cannot raise.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.

Only addOns/mcp was reviewed. The listener's bind address (Server.DEFAULT_ADDRESS), TLS handling, request size limits and ZAP's own modes and configuration permissions live in other add-ons or ZAP core and were not examined; localhost binding is inferred from the add-on help text.
C4 and C7 are structurally absent for this add-on; the total therefore includes two full-credit absent surfaces and the applicable score is the better comparison.
